subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 45-year-old man develops sudden right-sided facial weakness and notices that sweet and salty foods taste markedly diminished on the right anterior tongue. He can still bite, chew, and move his tongue normally, and light touch over the anterior tongue is intact.
question: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by which cranial nerve?

options.text: Mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3)

explanation_correct: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch. Taste fibers from this region travel in the chorda tympani, a branch of CN VII, which joins the lingual nerve before reaching the tongue; all taste fibers (VII, IX, X) project to the nucleus tractus solitarius. General sensation from the same region is carried by CN V3, which is intact here, explaining why touch is preserved. This patient's facial weakness localizes the lesion to CN VII (eg, Bell palsy), the classic cause of diminished anterior tongue taste.

explanation_incorrect.B: CN V3 (lingual nerve) carries general sensation, not taste, from the anterior two-thirds; a lesion there would cause numbness rather than an isolated loss of taste.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN IX supplies both taste and general sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN X provides taste and sensation to the extreme posterior tongue and motor supply to palatoglossus, not the anterior taste tested here.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN XII is purely motor to the tongue muscles (hyoglossus, genioglossus, styloglossus) and does not carry taste fibers.

educationalObjective: The 1st pharyngeal arch forms the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, with taste via CN VII and general sensation via CN V3.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 67-year-old woman has suffered a lateral medullary stroke. She reports that the back of her tongue feels numb and that salty and bitter tastes are diminished there, while the front of her tongue tastes normally.
question: Which cranial nerve provides both general sensation and taste to the posterior one-third of the tongue?
explanation_correct: The posterior one-third of the tongue arises from the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal arches and receives both general sensation and taste mainly via CN IX (glossopharyngeal). The extreme posterior tongue is the exception, supplied by CN X. Because taste and sensation are both lost over the posterior tongue with the anterior tongue spared, CN IX is the affected nerve. Like VII and X, CN IX taste fibers terminate in the nucleus tractus solitarius.

explanation_incorrect.A: CN V3 mediates general sensation only to the anterior two-thirds (1st arch) and does not serve the posterior tongue.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN VII carries taste from the anterior two-thirds via the chorda tympani; it does not provide general sensation there or serve the posterior tongue.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN X supplies only the extreme posterior tongue for taste and sensation, not the entire posterior one-third.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN XII innervates the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles and has no sensory or taste role.

educationalObjective: Taste and general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue travel via CN IX, with the extreme posterior region supplied by CN X.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 55-year-old man has extensive damage to both hypoglossal nerves, leaving him unable to protrude, retract, or depress his tongue. During swallowing, however, he can still elevate the posterior part of his tongue.
question: Which cranial nerve still supplies tongue motor function in this patient?
explanation_correct: CN XII innervates hyoglossus (retracts and depresses), genioglossus (protrudes), and styloglossus (draws the sides upward to form a swallowing trough); with both hypoglossal nerves damaged these actions are lost. Palatoglossus, which elevates the posterior tongue during swallowing, is the exception: it is supplied by CN X. Preserved elevation of the posterior tongue therefore indicates intact CN X function. Remember that CN 10 innervates palatoglossus.

explanation_incorrect.A: CN V3 provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and motor supply to muscles of mastication, not tongue elevation.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN VII carries taste from the anterior two-thirds and supplies muscles of facial expression; it does not innervate tongue musculature.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN IX provides taste and sensation to the posterior tongue and supplies stylopharyngeus, not palatoglossus.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN XII is damaged in this patient; it supplies hyoglossus, genioglossus, and styloglossus but not palatoglossus.

educationalObjective: CN XII supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus, which is innervated by CN X.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 62-year-old man with a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve is asked to stick out his tongue. The tongue deviates to the side of the lesion because the unaffected genioglossus acts unopposed.
question: Which cranial nerve provides motor supply to genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus?
explanation_correct: Motor innervation to the tongue is via CN XII to hyoglossus (retracts and depresses), genioglossus (protrudes), and styloglossus (draws the sides upward to create a trough for swallowing). The mnemonic 'the genie comes out of the lamp in style' links genioglossus to protrusion. With a unilateral CN XII lesion the intact genioglossus protrudes the tongue toward the weak side. Palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle supplied by CN X rather than CN XII.

explanation_incorrect.A: CN X supplies palatoglossus only, the muscle that elevates the posterior tongue during swallowing.
explanation_incorrect.C: CN IX carries posterior tongue taste and sensation and innervates stylopharyngeus, not these tongue muscles.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN V3 carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds and motor supply to muscles of mastication.
explanation_incorrect.E: CN VII carries anterior tongue taste and supplies facial expression muscles, not the tongue.

educationalObjective: CN XII drives genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus; a CN XII lesion makes the tongue deviate toward the lesion on protrusion.
